result:
Here is a small meditation on the present moment, memory, and the strange gift of language.

There is a particular quality of light in late afternoon, especially in autumn, that seems to carry the whole day with it. It is not the bright, declarative light of morning, which promises and asserts. Nor is it the harsh, vertical light of noon, which flattens the world into a map of itself. It is a sloping, amber light, almost liquid, that reaches into the corners of rooms and touches ordinary objects—a coffee cup, the spine of a book, a pair of glasses on the table—and makes them seem briefly important, as if they were props in a play we had forgotten we were in.

It is in these moments that I feel the strange texture of time. Not as a line, but as a kind of living material, folding over itself. I can be thirty-five and sitting in a borrowed chair, and also six and watching dust motes spiral in a shaft of light on my grandmother’s stairway, and also some future version of myself, looking back at this exact moment from a distance I cannot yet measure. All of these are present, somehow, in the same amber glow. Memory is not storage; it is a condition. We do not have memories. We are memory, woven into the current second.

And yet, the present moment—this one, right now, as I write these words—is the only thing that is truly real. Everything else is reconstruction or projection. The past is a story we tell ourselves, edited and revised with every retelling. The future is pure invention. The only honest place is here, in the act of attention. That is why writing matters to me. It is a practice of paying attention. A way of saying: *This, too, was real. This, too, was a moment that passed and will not come again.*

Language is a peculiar instrument for this task. It is both inadequate and inexhaustible. Inadequate, because no word can fully carry the weight of a sensation—the smell of rain on hot pavement, the specific ache of a goodbye, the warmth of a hand held when you did not expect it. And yet inexhaustible, because we keep trying. We keep arranging words in new orders, hoping that the right combination will finally make another person feel what we felt, see what we saw. Sometimes, impossibly, it works. A poem, a line of a song, a sentence in a novel—suddenly, a stranger’s words become your own buried thought. You are not alone anymore. The circuit of connection is complete.

This is what I love about the act of creation, in any form. It is a reaching across the dark. We are all separate, locked in the privacy of our own skulls, and yet we have built bridges out of sounds and marks on paper. We have made a shared world out of symbols. It is a fragile and ridiculous miracle. It is also the best thing we do.

If I were to give advice to anyone reading this, it would not be grand or original. It would simply be this: notice things. Keep a notebook. Write down the way the light looked, the thing the stranger said on the bus, the dream that faded before you could hold it. Not for fame. Not for publication. Just to mark the passing. Just to keep your attention alive.

Because attention is a kind of love. To truly see something is to honor it. And when you honor the small, ordinary moments of your life, you discover that they were never small or ordinary at all. They were the whole point. The coffee cup. The amber light. The dust motes in the stairwell. The hand that rests near yours on the table.

We are here for such a short while. The least we can do is pay attention.
